items.summary: The bloc seeks to avoid losing further ground to the United States and China in advanced technologies.

EU plans 50 billion euro investment in AI, quantum computing

The bloc seeks to avoid losing further ground to the United States and China in advanced technologies.

BRUSSELS: The European Union (EU) announced on Wednesday (Nov 25) plans to earmark up to 50 billion euros (US$55 billion) to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe, as the bloc seeks to avoid losing further ground to the United States and China in advanced technologies.

The fund would "ensure access to innovative funding instruments, not only for quantum technologies, but more widely for all critical technologies which are necessary to our tech sovereignty and economic security," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told a press conference at the European parliament in Strasbourg.

"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now 50 billion euros," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point".

Virkkunen unveiled the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" as she presented new rules to bolster quantum development in Europe.

Both the rules and fund are part of the bloc's broader efforts to cut dependency on US and other non-European technologies.

Quantum technology harnesses the power of quantum mechanics - laws that govern how physics operates at atomic and sub-atomic scales - to solve certain problems much faster than traditional computers.

The EU expects the impact of quantum computing to be "catalytic" in several areas, leading to breakthroughs on drugs, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries. Quantum could even accelerate AI development.

The new rules will push public authorities to favour European businesses for public money over non-EU firms.

But Virkkunen said Europe remained open to working with "like-minded international partners" in the quantum field.

"This is not a blanket requirement that every component be manufactured in the EU," the European Commission said.

The law would be adopted after negotiations between EU states and parliament.

LIMITED CAPITAL

Europe says it wants to be a global leader in quantum computing by 2030.

The bloc is already a world leader in quantum research but lags in translating this into viable commercial opportunities.

"Our industrial ecosystem is fragile due to fragmented support across the member states and also lower access to private capital compared to USA and China," Virkkunen said.

Quantum start-ups in Europe currently attract only five per cent of global private funding compared to 50 per cent in the United States, she said.

The EU says future benefits from quantum advances could include more secure communications for military and national security operations, or helping to develop more advanced defence equipment.

Despite its potential, quantum technologies also pose cybersecurity risks, such as breaking encryption and other systems protecting digital data, at a time when AI and cyberattacks are rattling governments and companies.

The European Commission last week said an AI-assisted cyberattack hit its systems in October, which came after hacks on store freezers across Europe that resulted in huge losses of food.

items.title: Fact check: Deepfakes and 'US abandons Taiwan' claims spread ahead of vote
items.summary: Ahead of local elections, Taiwan is seeing a surge in AI-generated attacks on mayoral candidate Puma Shen, alongside disinformation portraying the US as abandoning the island.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PguY

Prefer DW on Google

DPP supporters at a campaign event ahead of Taiwan's local elections, which have seen a rise in online disinformationImage: Cheng Yu-chen/AFP

Advertisement

On November 28, Taiwan will hold local elections that could reshape power dynamics between the sovereignty-leaning Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the Beijing-friendly Kuomintang (KMT). The outcome could influence relations between Taiwan and China, as well as regional geopolitics and ties between Washington, Beijing and Taipei.

A month before the election, there was a spike in AI-generated content featuring DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen. Claims that the US is abandoning Taiwan also increased during the same period. Experts say that fake quotes and misleading clips are being used as part of a campaign to weaken trust in US security commitments.

Did Trump offer to sell US arms to China?

The V-Dem Institute at the University of Gothenburg ranked Taiwan "the country most severely targeted" by foreign disinformation for eleven consecutive years – from 2014 to 2024.

The Taiwanese Ministry of the Interior has stated that foreign actors are increasingly using diverse methods to interfere in elections. That includes manipulating election betting, inviting Taiwanese citizens to China, using donations from Taiwanese business people to organize events, such as banquets, and leveraging temple and religious activities, to mobilize and win over supporters. Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence since 1949 despite Beijing's decadeslong claim to the island as a province and repeated vows to annex it.

DW Fact Check examined viral claims that have circulated online since September during the run-up to the election.

Deepfake audio, video target pro-sovereignty candidate

Claim: Puma Shen takes drug and receives kickbacks through arms purchases from the US.

DW Fact check: Fake

AI-generated audio recordings attacking DPP's Taipei mayoral candidate circulated on Facebook one month before Taiwan's local electionsImage: Facebook

An audio clip posted on Facebook on October 29, claims to show Puma Shen, the DPP candidate for Taipei mayor, admitting to receiving kickbacks from US arms deals.

The recording is heavy with background noise – a method used to mask synthetic manipulation in AI-generated audio. Multiple deepfake detection platforms, including Is this AI and Undetectable, flagged the audio as likely AI-generated.

The Facebook account that posted the audio was created on October 29, 2026 – the date the audio was also published. The account's followers are mainly profiles using languages, such as English, Arabic and Thai. That points to possible bot activity.

Another Facebook account posted an image of Puma Shen taking drugs. Apart from the "AI content" label on the post, multiple AI detector tools identified this photo as likely AI-generated.

Taiwanese independent media platform Watchout discovered that the advertiser behind this Facebook account is located in ChinaImage: Facebook

The account was created in March 2026. Since then, a lot of AI-generated content mocking Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te and his pro-sovereignty party has been posted. It is occasionally interspersed with posts praising the development of Chinese cities.

This account's profile indicates that the primary country location for people who manage this page includes China and Taiwan.

Taiwanese independent media platform Watchout investigated the account's advertising activity and found that it had previously run at least five Facebook ads. The advertisers were identified as Peng Zhiwei and Guo Yang, both based in China. The findings suggest that the account received financial support from individuals in China.

The AI detection tool "AI or Not" indicates that this photo is likely AI-generatedImage: aiornot.com

The Taipei mayoral race is a key battleground in Taiwan's upcoming local elections. As of mid-November, polls showed a neck-and-neck contest between Puma Shen and his opponent, Chiang Wan-an, who claims to be a great-grandson of Taiwanese leader Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang Kai-shek was a leading figure of the Kuomintang and relocated with the party to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese Civil War to the Chinese Communist Party.

While the Kuomintang was historically staunchly anti-communist, critics argue that it now promotes closer ties with China. For example, they point to a senior Kuomintang figure's proposed 10-year unification framework as evidence that its stance runs counter to mainstream public opinion in Taiwan. Although the Kuomintang subsequently stated that this framework is entirely unrelated to the current party leadership, it has sparked controversy in Taiwan.

Distorted quotes and misleading clips

Claim: A TikTok video claims to show US president Donald Trump saying the US is abandoning Taiwan.

DW Fact check: Misleading

In this TikTok video, Donald Trump's response in an interview was interpreted beyond what the US president had actually saidImage: tiktok.com

The original video was from a Fox News interview with Trump on May 16. The interviewer did not ask whether the United States would defend Taiwan, and the US president did not comment on the issue.

Trump said he did not want Taiwan to become independent or for a war to break out, adding that the status quo should be maintained to allow tensions to de-escalate. He also clearly stated that his policy toward Taiwan "has not changed." Washington has long maintained a policy of strategic ambiguity toward Taiwan– neither explicitly guaranteeing the island's defense nor ruling out the possibility of doing so.

Correction from November 25, 2026: A previous version of this article (published on November 25, 2025) included an example referring to headlines on search engines claiming that US troops were withdrawing from Taiwan. This has been removed because while they were sensational, they were not entirely wrong because they referred to a report by a thinktank. We apologize for the error.

The economic cost of a Taiwanese invasion

items.title: Protesters call on Israel to free Palestinian student held without charge
items.summary: Mahdi Tunsi, 26, was taken from his university dormitory earlier this month and has since been held without charge.
items.body:
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Mahdi Tunsi appears by videolink in front of his attorney Nasser Odeh during his hearing at the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday

ByKaty Watson

Reporting fromEast Jerusalem

Israeli students, activists and academics are calling for the release of a Palestinian undergraduate who was taken from his university dormitory by Israeli police earlier this month and has since been held without charge.

Mahdi Tunsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, appeared in an Israeli court in the city on Tuesday - a hearing that was held behind closed doors.

Israeli police say he was arrested "concerning ties to an act of terrorism".

Authorities have requested what is known as "administrative detention", which allows the Israeli state to detain people indefinitely without charge on the basis of secret evidence that they cannot see.

"We definitely think this is a political arrest," said Dr Yael Berda, one of Tunsi's university professors.

Tunsi, a Palestinian resident of occupied East Jerusalem who works with well-known Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, was arrested a month after Israel held an election that saw Arab-led parties win a record 19 seats in parliament, the Knesset, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition lose its majority.

Since then, Berda said she had seen an intensifying campaign against Palestinian rights.

Image caption,

Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the court

Outside the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday, demonstrators waved placards with a black-and-white image of Tunsi, while crying out "shame" in unison.

"There's no due process - [administrative detention is] a sugar-coated term for being kidnapped and held as a hostage," said Dr Ofer Cassif, a Member of the Knesset representing the Arab-led Joint List alliance.

"We must all stand firm against such crimes. It's unacceptable."

Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, the number of people in administrative detention has more than doubled.

In October, there were more than 3,100 in administrative detention, according to Israel Prison Service figures published by Israeli rights group HaMoked. Most of them are Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.

Israel says that its use of the policy is compliant with international law and a necessary preventative measure to combat terrorism.

Image caption,

Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and Hebrew

In a statement, Israeli police said they would "not elaborate further regarding the investigation" into Tunsi.

He appeared via video link from prison - his hair and beard shaved off. His friends also said that he was without medication as well as his glasses, despite a judge requesting them to be brought to him in detention.

The Israel Prison Service said it acted in accordance with the court's rulings.

"When the process was complete and all the necessary approvals had been received, the detainee's lawyer was told he could pass the eyeglasses to the detainee immediately, subject to security procedures," it added.

Berda asked to enter the courtroom on Tuesday but was denied entry. According to Berda, not even Tunsi has been told of the evidence against him.

The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention. A decision is expected in the coming days.

Image caption,

The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention

"If they have evidence, have them bring it or release him," said Berda.

"That's why we're demanding his immediate release or moving it to a criminal track where he could defend himself."

Berda said that while Tunsi could not vote in Israel's general election because he is not an Israeli citizen, he was "engaged" and very supportive of Arab parties' involvement.

"Mahdi is one of the best human beings I know," said Noga Kaplan, who studies with him at the Hebrew University.

"He has a really pure heart and is very passionate about his studies."

Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.

After Tunsi's arrest, the Hebrew University issued a statement saying it was notified a few minutes before it took place.

"The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings," it said.

It added that it was concerned for Tunsi's well-being and hoped "that the matter will be resolved promptly and that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process".

Tunsi is a resident of Silwan, a neighbourhood in East Jerusalem where, in recent years, Palestinians have been evicted by Israeli authorities, who say their properties were built illegally. Israeli settlers have since moved into some of those properties.

"Political organisation stopped after October 7 because people were getting super scared about the consequences," explained Kaplan.

"Mahdi saw studying as one of the ways to speak about it in class."

"He didn't do a lot of public stuff because what's happening now is his biggest fear."

items.title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
items.summary: The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
items.body:
Asia

China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining

November 25, 20264:44 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025.

Ng Han Guan/AP

hide caption

Ng Han Guan/AP

BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.

The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.

Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.

A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.

The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.

"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."

The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.

"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."

Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.

items.title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
items.summary: Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
items.body:
Sports

Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco

November 25, 20261:43 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Senegal's Sadio Mane holds the trophy aloft as he celebrates with teammates after winning the Africa Cup of Nations final soccer match between Senegal and Morocco in Rabat, Morocco, Sunday, Jan. 18, 2026.

Youssef Loulidi/AP

hide caption

Youssef Loulidi/AP

More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.

Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.

Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.

CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.

The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."

Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Morocco raises concerns over CAS process

Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.

In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.

Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."

CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.

Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.

Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."

Sports

European nations say World Cup boycott is still on, keeping FIFA's Infantino in limbo

Trouble on the field and in the stands

Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.

The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.

Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.

The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.

Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.

Soccer's laws versus regulations

Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.

The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.

In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."

The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.

The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.

Soccer fans in Senegal celebrate a win

"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.

Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.

"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.

"At the end of the day Morocco and Senegal are brothers," Sidibé added, referring to the countries' long shared close ties built on religion, trade and culture.

Sidi Sylla, a philosophy student at Dakar's main university, said the court's ruling was "not just a win for Senegal but for football in general."

Historic decision

CAS rulings have stripped many athletes of Olympic medals for doping, but it's rare to overturn the result of a major soccer competition.

CAS refused to change the results of the 2019 Asian Cup, dismissing an appeal that the star striker on winning team Qatar shouldn't have been eligible for the tournament.

A lengthy legal battle over the same year's African Champions League final also ended with the original winner, Esperance of Tunisia, taking the title after its opponent Wydad from Morocco refused to play on.

One notable CAS ruling on a team sport title came at the Winter Olympics in 2022. A doping case involving then-15-year-old Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva ended up with her disqualification, and the Russian team being dropped from gold to bronze in the team event.

3 dead as Indonesian rescuers search for 'estimated' 23 more workers trapped in mine

Heavy rain cuts off a 100m-deep West Java mine, with workers feared trapped since Monday as rescuers battle narrow, dark access.

JAKARTA: Three people have died while search and rescue operations are currently underway for an "estimated" 23 more workers trapped in a mine in West Java province on Wednesday (Nov 25), authorities said.

The miners have been stuck in a mine 100m deep since Monday as heavy rains inundated access, the search and rescue agency said, adding access was narrow and the terrain was slippery and dark.

"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement.

The agency said the first body was recovered at 12.20pm (local time), followed by the second at 12.35pm and the third at 1.48pm.

The Jakarta SAR Office is coordinating with joint rescue teams to monitor flooding and assess access to the mine shaft in Kampung Ciguha, Nanggung, Bogor Regency. (Photo: Basarnas)

The agency said it was pumping water out of the mine shaft to support search and evacuation efforts.

The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital Jakarta.

State miner Antam, which operates gold mining operations in Pongkor, said the incident occurred at an unauthorised gold mine and was not a part of its operations.

Small-scale and illegal mining has often caused accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate.

Authorities closed around 30 gold mine pits last week in a separate area in Bogor, news website Detik reported.

Australia, Solomon Islands sign sweeping pact stymieing China

The treaty cements Australia as the island nation's "primary security partner" and will see Canberra commit US$490 million over a decade to fund free education and other programmes.

CANBERRA: Solomon Islands and Australia signed a sweeping treaty on Wednesday (Nov 25), affirming there will be no foreign military base in the Pacific nation in a deal seen as a blow to China's ambitions in the region.

Prime Minister Matthew Wale and 15 ministers visited Canberra for talks spanning security, infrastructure, education and health.

"Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region," Wale told journalists alongside Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese.

"Those days are gone."

The treaty cements Australia as the island nation's "primary security partner" and will see Canberra commit AU$740 million ($490 million) over a decade to fund free education and other programs.

It affirms the "sovereign decision" by the Solomon Islands that there will be no foreign military or security base on its soil.

Solomon Islands' "sensitive" infrastructure will also "remain free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access".

The treaty text shows that will span airports, ports, energy and telecommunications - where China has built infrastructure under million-dollar loans since the country switched ties from Taiwan in 2019 - but the clause will not be applied retrospectively.

The Solomon Islands will also be required to consult with Australia before making deals with other countries on critical infrastructure or security cooperation outside members of the Pacific Islands Forum regional bloc, Albanese said.

He praised the deal as a "new chapter in our partnership to strengthen our shared prosperity and our security".

Wale has been in a diplomatic sprint since he was elected leader in May, upending close ties with Beijing built by predecessor Manasseh Sogavare and travelling to Canberra and Washington to rebuild relationships with traditional partners.

Asked about reports he had ended a secretive security pact with Beijing, Wale told journalists that discussions with China were "ongoing".

He could not comment further due to a non-disclosure clause in the deal.

China's foreign ministry on Tuesday said its ties with Pacific nations were not matters of "geopolitical contests".

Prime Minister of Solomon Islands Matthew Wale (left) and Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese after a signing ceremony in Parliament House in Canberra on Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Saeed Khan)

CHINA FEARS

Struck in 2022, the pact had "caught Canberra unprepared for a new era of intense geopolitical competition with China in Australia's immediate neighbourhood," Mihai Sora, director of research at the Lowy Institute think tank, said.

The Solomons hosted Chinese police and Australia grew anxious the deal also covered the Chinese navy.

The pact "made real the prospect of a persistent Chinese military presence some 1,600KM off the coast of Australia," Sora, a former Australian diplomat in the Solomons, told AFP.

It "was the catalyst for the past four years of frenetic Australian diplomacy in the region in an attempt to stem further strategic damage," he added.

Australia countered by striking security alliances or wide-ranging treaties with another five Pacific island countries.

Wale adjourned the Solomons parliament indefinitely in September after staring down a no-confidence vote.

He was forced to abruptly leave a Pacific leaders' summit in Palau to stop the attempt to bring down his new coalition government on the eve of a visit by the US Deputy Secretary of State.

Prime Minister of Solomon Islands Matthew Wale during a press conference in Canberra on Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Saeed Khan)

REFORMS EXPECTED

Solomons officials told AFP on Wednesday that parliament will return in January to approve significant reforms, including a pledge for free education.

A third of Solomon Islands children don't start school, and only 19 per cent finish because of the cost.

The Australian funds will be in place by January, bolstering Wale's government as parliament returns.

Over a decade, Australia will provide A$670 million in grants and A$70 million in concessional loans to boost education, health, policing, resources and climate resilience.

The treaty also covers road and bridge construction - areas China has dominated in the islands through its Belt and Road Initiative.

Wale said the decision to approve the Australian treaty was taken by his entire cabinet, many of whom had travelled to Canberra for the signing.

Solomons opposition party leader, Sogavare on Tuesday criticised the "fast-tracking" of the treaty with Australia while the status of China security arrangement remained "unclear".

The treaty cements Australia as the island nation's "primary security partner" and will see Canberra commit AU$740 million ($490 million) over a decade to fund free education and other programs.
It affirms the "sovereign decision" by the Solomon Islands that there will be no foreign military or security base on its soil.
Solomon Islands' "sensitive" infrastructure will also "remain free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access".

The treaty text shows that will span airports, ports, energy and telecommunications - where China has built infrastructure under million-dollar loans since the country switched ties from Taiwan in 2019 - but the clause will not be applied retrospectively.

The Solomon Islands will also be required to consult with Australia before making deals with other countries on critical infrastructure or security cooperation outside members of the Pacific Islands Forum regional bloc, Albanese said.
He praised the deal as a "new chapter in our partnership to strengthen our shared prosperity and our security".

Estonia warns of growing Russian hybrid threats, to close remaining road border crossings

Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia from Dec 1 for at least six months, citing security concerns after accusing Moscow of orchestrating two attempted arson attacks on its defence companies this year.

SAATSE, Estonia: In a remote corner of southeastern Estonia, a narrow stretch of road offers a stark reminder of the Baltic nation's complicated relationship with its much larger neighbour, Russia.

The road passes through the Saatse Boot, a roughly 115ha slice of Russian territory that protrudes into Estonia.

Named for its distinctive boot-like shape, the section cuts across about 1km of the Varska-Ulitina road, which connects several Estonian villages near the border.

This left motorists with an unusual choice: take a detour of nearly 20km, or pass briefly through Russian territory without a visa or border checks, provided they did not stop.

Even during a vehicle breakdown, drivers had to remain inside and contact Estonian border guards for assistance. Stepping onto Russian soil could constitute illegal entry into the country.

But that arrangement came to an abrupt halt in October 2025, when Estonia closed the route after armed Russian military personnel were spotted in the vicinity.

Authorities accelerated the construction of bypass roads to skirt around the boot, allowing drivers to avoid Russian territory.

For a country sharing a roughly 340km border with Russia, the episode illustrates how even a tiny geographical anomaly can become a security concern amid heightened tensions between Moscow and the West.

INCREASED VIGILANCE ALONG THE BORDER

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Estonia has stepped up efforts to secure its increasingly sensitive frontier.

“We've made changes to our training systems just to be more ready if some sort of crisis happens here,” said Renet Merdikes, head of the Saatse Border Guard Station, whose team patrols nearly a third of the border.

Estonian border guards patrol along the border with Russia near Saatse. (Image: CNA)

A barbed-wire fence along the border between Estonia and Russia. (Image: CNA)

A road leading into Russia is closed off at the Estonian side of the border. (Image: CNA)

Remote Saatse is far removed from Estonia's major population centres – it is more than 280km from the capital Tallinn. But the proximity of Russian military activity is a regular reminder of the potential risks.

Residents frequently hear Russian military exercises taking place across the border while Estonian guards closely monitor developments.

But officials say the more immediate threat is not necessarily a conventional military incursion, but less visible forms of interference. These include the jamming of surveillance drones, which border guards say occurs almost daily.

Such incidents form part of a broader pattern of hybrid warfare, ranging from cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns to sabotage and electronic interference, aimed at destabilising an adversary without outright military confrontation.

SUSPECTED SABOTAGE RAISES ALARM

Estonian authorities have accused Russia of orchestrating a series of sabotage operations targeting the country's defence industry.

In August, officials blamed Moscow for an arson attack on Tallinn-based Milrem Robotics, which manufactures unmanned vehicles, some of which have been deployed to Ukraine.

Estonian defence company Milrem Robotics, which authorities say was targeted in a Russia-linked arson attack in August. (Image: CNA)

Estonia also said it thwarted an attempted arson attack on defence company Threod Systems on Nov 14, which authorities attributed to Russia's GRU military intelligence agency.

In response, Estonia announced it would close its three remaining road border crossings with Russia from Dec 1 for at least six months, saying the move would help address security concerns and limit further attacks.

Moscow has denied involvement in the arson attacks and vowed to respond with political and diplomatic measures, accusing Tallinn of trying to ‌“erect a new Iron Curtain”.

The incidents have fuelled concerns that Russia could step up covert attacks against defence manufacturers and critical infrastructure.

Estonian police and border guard service members watch as travellers walk to the border crossing point with Russia in Narva, Estonia, Nov 17, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Janis Laizans)

EU, Estonian and NATO flags flutter near a bridge over the Narva River at the border crossing point with Russia in Narva, Estonia, Nov 17, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Janis Laizans)

A pedestrian walks past Estonia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is flying both the Estonia and Ukraine flags, in Tallinn, Nov 24, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Janis Laizans)

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna warned that Russia could escalate its provocations to test the resolve of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).

“We will probably see something more serious like terror attacks or sabotage, anything against NATO to test and push the lines,” he said.

“Estonia is pretty resilient about that, but my question is whether the other capitals in Europe are.”

During a visit to Estonia last month, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sought to reassure allies that such incidents would not weaken the alliance's resolve.

“We will react when we need to react. The most important thing is to … stay calm, carry on, invest in defence,” he said.

He also reiterated the need to ensure Ukraine receives the military assistance it requires.

DRONE THREATS ACROSS EUROPE

Across Europe, reports of suspicious drone activity near airports, military installations and other critical infrastructure have prompted governments to strengthen their counter-drone capabilities.

In Germany, authorities have linked Russia to suspected drone incidents at Leipzig/Halle Airport. In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes. The device reportedly failed to explode because of a faulty detonator.

Investigators also suspected that a second drone had collided with a cargo aircraft nearby, while a third was reportedly discovered near the airport about 10 days later.

Russian President Vladimir Putin rejected the allegations, accusing Germany of planting evidence to implicate Moscow.

A police officer in protective gear is seen next to an explosive-disarming robot (EOD) at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Schkeuditz, Germany, Aug 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Axel Schmidt)

The incidents have added urgency to European efforts to improve drone detection and defence systems.

Netherlands-based Robin Radar Systems is among the companies working with Ukrainian forces and several NATO allies to counter the threat.

“We've seen a lot of unknown drone movements close to our coast, airports (and) some military air bases,” said its chief commercial officer Marcel Verdonk.

“That increased threat has (made) all of us realise that we need to invest in counter-drone equipment to detect what's happening and also figure out ways to deal with it.”

CALLS FOR TOUGHER MEASURES AGAINST RUSSIA

Estonia has been pressing European governments for a tougher, more coordinated response to Russian hybrid threats.

Saatse border guard chief Merdikes said Estonian border guards have been deployed to assist neighbouring Latvia in responding to what authorities describe as hybrid attacks involving Russian ally Belarus.

Estonian Interior Minister Igor Taro speaks during an interview with CNA. (Image: CNA)

Tallinn is also backing calls for an European Union-wide ban on Russian tourist visas, arguing that such travel poses security risks.

However, European countries remain divided, with France, Italy and Spain among those continuing to issue visas to eligible Russian travellers.

Because much of continental Europe operates under the Schengen system, visas issued by one member state can generally allow travel across other participating countries, subject to applicable entry restrictions.

“It's not only a moral question on how you can let Russians go shopping in Paris when Ukrainians are dying every day,” Estonian Interior Minister Igor Taro told CNA.

“It's also a question about security because (Russia is) using these tourists – their citizens – for hybrid attacks.”

Taro said Putin had severely misjudged Ukraine's ability and determination to defend itself, as well as the international support it would receive, and warned that an even greater danger lies in Moscow doing so again.

“He (Putin) miscalculated by a large scale. He thought Ukraine had nothing to fight with – no resources, no army. He thought the Ukrainians were not willing to fight. (Another) miscalculation was that he thought that no one would help,” Taro said.

“The biggest risk is that they (the Russians) can do it again. Obviously, Putin is not getting the real information from the frontline … or they would be out already. That's why they are still hoping to achieve something.”

Russia-Ukraine war widens in the Black Sea in a test of NATO red lines

Commentary: Ukraine is doing better. Now it's Europe's turn

RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said on Wednesday (Nov 25) it had struck Yemen's Hodeida after the Iran-backed group threatened to retaliate against the kingdom's Red Sea ports if the attack took place.

The coalition, which support Yemen's internationally recognised government, renewed fighting in July against the Iran-backed fighters, who control swathes of the country, including Hodeida.

"We targeted operational capabilities at the port of Hodeidah," the Saudi-led coalition posted on X.

Riyadh had instructed civilians in Hodeida to evacuate in a social media post early on Wednesday.

The Houthi's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, had earlier threatened Saudi Arabia with retaliation in the event of an attack.

"The port of Jeddah, along with all other Saudi enemy ports along the Red Sea coast, will become targets for our forces should the enemy carry out its threats to bombard the port of Hodeidah," he posted on Telegram on Wednesday.

Saudi skyscraper hit again, coalition slams 'terrorist attack'

Houthi media outlet Almasirah reported an "attack on the port of Hodeida", without providing further details. No casualties or injuries have been reported.

Almasirah added that Saudi forces had also attacked the area's international airport.

Saree warned civilians near Saudi ports to "evacuate immediately and keep their distance" and called for "all shipping companies to remove their vessels from these ports at once".

The Saudi capital's tallest skyscraper was struck for a second time in days on Tuesday, wounding 11 people. The coalition called it a "terrorist attack" and blamed the strike on the Houthis.

Qatar and Pakistan, who have been acting as mediators in efforts to end the wider Middle East conflict between Iran and the United States both "strongly" condemned the attack on the tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund.

Two Indian citizens were wounded, the South Asian nation's foreign ministry said, adding such attacks "seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability."

The building had already been attacked last Thursday and is one of several high-profile targets hit since fighting with the Iran-backed group reignited in July.

The Saudi capital's tallest skyscraper was struck for a second time in days on Tuesday, wounding 11 people. The coalition called it a "terrorist attack" and blamed the strike on the Houthis.

Two Indian citizens were wounded, the South Asian nation's foreign ministry said, adding such attacks "seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability."

Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO

Nvidia’s board faces scrutiny after unanimously rehiring Jensen Huang days after accepting his resignation, fuelling calls for accountability and transparency.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs after a welcome ceremony with President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People, on May 14, 2026, in Beijing. (Photo: AP/Mark Schiefelbein)

Read a summary of this article on FAST.

FAST

NEW YORK: Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the company's board is joining him at the centre of scrutiny.

The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia's president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and "input from senior levels of the United States government". President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.

Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.

“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.

The board's stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump's role means for the meeting of business and politics.

CONCERNS SWIRL

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at big-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.

Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.

Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.

“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she said.

Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.

“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”

It’s not unusual for US tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.

American business has a culture of “leader heroes” - entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance".

Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang is back, but questions facing Nvidia remain, say analysts

Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.

“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”

The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window" if the sitting president "essentially tells them what to do," said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.

“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.

Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives" in their relationships with businesses.

LAWMAKERS CALL FOR ACCOUNTABILITY

The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang's affair raised questions about Nvidia's compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervour on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.

Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and scepticism.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was "reckless". She wrote in a statement on Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board “still owe Congress answers".

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang's affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president's intervention "does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favour".

The California Department of Justice said on Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang said he violated code of conduct, source says

Commentary: Jensen Huang should never have been too big to fail at Nvidia

SOME MEMBERS JOINED NVIDIA BOARD IN 1990s

Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.

Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.

Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.

Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.

Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.

John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.

None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press.

Source: AP/ec

items.title: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
items.summary: Beau Lamarre was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his ex Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies.
items.body:
Image source, NSW Supreme Court

Image caption,

Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau Lamarre

ByHelen Livingstone

Sydney

It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird

Image caption,

Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down

During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.

One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.

"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.

Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.

One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.

Dark infatuation

Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.

After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.

But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.

On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.

He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.

'The beginning of the plan for murder'

Image source, EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock

Image caption,

Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020

His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".

He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.

In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.

While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.

But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.

On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.

Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."

Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird

Image caption,

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.

But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.

The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".

Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.

Covering tracks

After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".

One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".

Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.

Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".

Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.

"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.

The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

Image source, NSW Supreme Court

Image caption,

Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.

On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.

His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."

Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.

Lamarre faces life in prison

Image source, Getty

Image caption,

The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney

By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."

"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."

He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.

Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.

The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.

Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

• Australia

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.
He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.
'The beginning of the plan for murder'

blocks.alt: A young man in police uniform raises his arms in the air standing in front of a crowd

blocks.text: Image source, EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Image caption,
Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020
His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".
He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.

In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.
While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.
But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.
On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.
Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."

blocks.alt: Two young men wearing pink holding drinks smile at the camera

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird
Image caption,
Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.
But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.
The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".
Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.
Covering tracks
After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".
One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".
Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.
Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".
Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.
"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.
The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

blocks.alt: One man holds up a surfboard bag against another in a sports store

blocks.text: Image source, NSW Supreme Court
Image caption,
Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.
On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.
His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."
Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.
Lamarre faces life in prison

blocks.alt: A grey painted town house with dozens of bunches of flowers in the railings outside

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
Image caption,
The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney
By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."
"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."
He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.
Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.
The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.
Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

items.title: Thomas Markle charged in US for possessing child sex abuse images
items.summary: The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
items.body:
Image source, Pinellas County Sheriff's Office

BySareen Habeshian

Reporting fromLos Angeles

Updated 3 hours ago

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.

The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.

Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.

The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.

US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.

His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.

Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.

The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.

Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.

"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.
